name: Real-Time Voice Conversion
title: Real-Time Voice Conversion
answer: Real-time voice conversion takes a live vocal input and re-synthesizes it as a different target voice with latency low enough that the performer hears the result while still singing. In the operatic context it sits alongside related work in vocal synthesis, where the aim is not to replace the singer but to change or extend the voice that reaches the audience. The scope covers both the signal problem, keeping delay under the threshold where a performer can still monitor themselves, and the musical problem, preserving pitch, vibrato, diction and phrasing through the conversion. It is distinct from text-to-speech, which generates a voice from written words rather than from a live performance.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The pipeline runs on a capture chain, usually a microphone into an audio interface, then a host machine with a low-latency audio driver and a graphics processor doing the neural inference. The conversion model itself is typically a small encoder that extracts pitch and content from the incoming signal and a decoder that renders them in the target timbre, with a vocoder producing the final waveform. Because the whole loop must fit inside a few tens of milliseconds, the model is kept compact and the buffer sizes are set aggressively small. The site tracks 2,000 audio models, and a working share of those are built for exactly this streaming, low-latency setting rather than for offline rendering.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Preparation starts with a reference recording of the target voice, often a short set of sustained notes and phrases, which is used to build or adapt the timbre model. The performer then sings into the system while hearing the converted output in headphones, adjusting technique to the voice they are wearing. Engineers tune the trade-off between latency, stability and naturalness, since pushing any one of the three tends to cost the other two. In performance the operator watches for artifacts at phrase boundaries and for drift in pitch tracking, and may switch presets between numbers. The result is a live instrument, played by a singer, that happens to sound like someone else.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The central issue is consent: converting a performance into a specific person's voice requires that person's permission, and in many jurisdictions a distinctive voice carries protection similar to a name or likeness. Rights in a recorded reference voice belong to the performer and often to a label or publisher as well, so a licence for the recording is not automatically a licence for the synthesis. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of them involving AI music services, which shows how unsettled this ground still is. Provenance practice is emerging around watermarking and signed metadata that record which model produced a voice and on whose authority, so that a converted performance can be traced after the fact.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Latency and naturalness keep improving, and the near-term direction is conversion that survives a full operatic phrase without audible seams or loss of diction. Beyond that, the interesting question is compositional: whether a singer can carry more than one voice within a single role, or shift timbre as a deliberate expressive choice rather than a technical effect. Houses and studios will need practical conventions for crediting a converted voice, and those conventions are likely to be shaped by the litigation now working through the courts. The technology is unlikely to remove the singer from the stage, but it does change what a single voice can be asked to do.
